cognate: *sóh₂wl̥ (genitive) 'sun' in every anchor; Gk κύκλος = Ved. cakrá- = ON hvél < *kʷékʷlos (Vedic and Norse only in support); Lat. rota = Ved. rátha- < *Hróth₂-eh₂/-os.
drift_or_renewal: There are two ways of saying 'wheel' here. (a) *kʷékʷlos, kept as 'wheel' in Gk κύκλος ἀελίοιο, Ved. sū́ryasya cakrám, ON fagrahvél 'fair wheel' (a name for the sun). (b) *Hróth₂-, which stays 'wheel' in Lat. solis rota but has drifted to 'chariot' in Indo-Iranian (AVŚ 13.2.15 sūryo ... rathe, the sun's chariot drawn by seven mares). The Greek and Latin anchors therefore do not share the wheel word: Latin rota renews κύκλος, and the cognate Latin/Vedic pair is rota/ratha. That wheel>chariot drift is the expected pars-pro-toto move.
shared_syntax: Genitive of the sun's name + head noun 'wheel' (Gk κύκλος ἀελίοιο, Lat. solis rota, Ved. sū́ryasya cakrám). In Vedic the drifted sense 'chariot' takes the sun as owner or rider (sūryo ... rathe, sūrya ... rathāya).
context: In all three the sun's disc is described as a wheel or wheeled vehicle moving across the sky. Euripides: the shining wheel of the sun with winged horses on Achilles' shield. Lucretius: the size and visibility of the solis rota. AVŚ 13.2: hymn to the sun yoking its mares to the chariot that circles both ends of the world. The Vedic support (Indra tearing off the sun's wheel) and ON fagrahvél show this is a fixed traditional image, not a simile made up on the spot.
phrase: *sh₂uens kʷékʷlos (pie-lex-soh2wl + pie-lex-kwekwlos) 'wheel of the sun', with the variant *sh₂uens Hróth₂eh₂ (pie-lex-Hroth2eh2)

cognate: Sun-name *sóh₂wl̥ (Ἠέλιος / sūra-) as subject; *médʰyo- 'middle' as goal (μέσον / vi-madhyam); and the same 'go' verb in the perfect (βαίνω ~ gam-: ἀμφιβέβηκε / jagāma).
drift_or_renewal: The thing whose middle is reached differs: Greek has οὐρανόν 'sky', Vedic has ádhvanaḥ 'of the road' (Aeschylus' μέσον πόρον 'mid-passage' comes closer to the Vedic). The verbs belong to the same inherited suppletive verb but not to one stem. Gk βαίνω is from *gʷm̥-yé-, while its perfect βέβηκα is built on *gʷeh₂- (ἔβην). Ved. jagā́ma is the perfect of *gʷem-. So the verb match is at the level of the lexeme and of the tense (perfect = 'has reached and stands there'), not an exact stem equation.
shared_syntax: Intransitive clause marking the time of day: sun (subject) + perfect of 'go' + accusative of goal 'the middle (of sky/road)'. Gk ἀμφι-βέβηκε μέσον οὐρανόν vs Ved. jagā́ma ... ví-madhyam.
context: In both the clause dates an action to noon. Il. 8.68 (= 16.777, Od. 4.400): 'when the Sun had bestridden mid-heaven, then the Father raised the scales'. AVŚ 7.72.3 = RV 10.179.2: 'the oblation is cooked; come, Indra; the sun has gone to the mid-point of its road', the midday offering. On chance: 'the sun stood at noon' is a universal idea, so this rests on the shared choice of a perfect of the *gʷem-/*gʷeh₂- verb with *médʰyo- as goal, the same tense value, and the same time-marking role. Taken one by one each word is common, which is why this is not rated high.
phrase: *sóh₂wl̥ médʰyom (…) gʷe-gʷóm-e 'the sun has gone to the middle (of its course)' (pie-lex-soh2wl + pie-lex-medhyos + pie-root-gwem-come)

cognate: Verb *derḱ- 'see': Ved. dr̥ś- (dr̥śé, dr̥śan) = Gk δέρκομαι (perfect δεδορκότες). Object *sóh₂wl̥ 'sun': Ved. sū́rya-/svàr = Latv. saule (= Gk ἥλιος in the Homeric variant).
drift_or_renewal: Greek keeps the verb and renews the object: φῶς/φάος 'light'. (φῶς is in the context line just before the passage line of Hercules 564; the δεδορκ- + φάος pairing is repeated in Hipp. and Alc.) Homer keeps the object (φάος ἠελίοιο) and renews the verb with ὁράω. Latvian keeps the object and renews the verb (redzēt). Splitting the two members between different renewals is the usual pattern for an inherited collocation.
shared_syntax: Transitive 'see' + sun/light as object, used as a periphrasis for being alive. Positive: Ved. svàr dr̥śé (dative infinitive, 'so as to see the sun'), Gk φῶς ... δεδορκότες. Negative: Ved. mā́ dr̥śan sū́ryam 'may they not see the sun', Latv. neredz sauli 'does not see the sun'.
context: RV 1.112.5: the Aśvins raised Vandana up out of the pit 'to see the sun', a rescue from death. Euripides Hercules 563-564: Heracles tells his family, brought back from the brink of death, to cast off the trappings of Hades and look up at the light, out of the darkness below. That is the same image of a return from the underworld to the light. RV 7.104.24 is a curse: 'may they not see the sun rising', i.e. may they die. The Latvian daina, 'sees neither sun nor moon' among the in-laws, uses the negative version for a joyless existence like death. Ved. jyók sū́ryaṃ dr̥śé 'to see the sun long' = long life, and Homeric ζώει καὶ ὁρᾷ φάος ἠελίοιο confirm that 'see the sun' = 'live' is fixed phraseology in both traditions.
phrase: *derḱ- + *sóh₂wl̥ (pie-root-derkj-see + pie-lex-soh2wl) 'to see the sun' = to be alive

cognate: Gk εὔχομαι / ἐπεύχομαι = Lat. uoueo, uotum < *h₁wegʷʰ- 'speak solemnly, vow' (the packet maps εὔχομαι to pie-lex-h1eh1ughtor; the root is pie-root-h1wegwh-promise, and Latin uotum is unmapped in the packet).
drift_or_renewal: In Latin the verb has narrowed to 'vow, promise to a god'. In Greek it has 'pray' and 'claim, boast' (Il. 2.82, Od. 21.335 in this packet). The deity is named in the dative in both: Gk θεοῖς, Lat. Marti Siluano.
shared_syntax: Verb (or verbal noun) *h₁wegʷʰ- + dative of the god addressed, in instructions. Gk imperative θεοῖς εὔχου, Lat. uotum ... facito / uouere.
context: Both are directions on how to address the gods. Theognis 171: 'pray to the gods, with the gods lies power'. Septem 266: Eteocles tells the women how to pray. Cato 83.1 prescribes the formal vow to Mars Silvanus for the health of the cattle. The overlap is the religious register and the cognate verb. But 'pray to the gods' with any inherited 'pray' verb is close to automatic, and the contexts are not specific (the Greek is general piety, the Latin a farm ritual). So this is a lexical-register survival more than a shaped formula.
phrase: *h₁wegʷʰ- + dative of deity (pie-root-h1wegwh-promise + pie-lex-dheh1s) 'to make a solemn utterance/vow to a god'

support.locus: PlAsina (LASLA), 'dies noctesque potent'; 'noctes et dies hunc annum totum'

cognate: Both members: Ved. nakta-/nákt- = Lat. nox < *nókʷts; Ved. dívā = Lat. diēs (*dyew-/*dyeh₂-). (Both words are in the context line before the passage line of each anchor; Ved. naktaṃ is unmapped in the packet.)
drift_or_renewal: Greek keeps 'night' and renews 'day' (νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ). Order varies: Vedic usually has day first (dívā náktam), Plautus has both orders.
shared_syntax: Two-word time merism of 'day' and 'night' used adverbially for 'at all times' (Ved. adverbs divā naktaṃ; Lat. accusatives noctes que dies que, written noctesque diesque).
context: AVP 12.18.19 asks 'whoever harmed you by day or night' and is followed by a request to Agni to burn him. Plautus Amph. 168 complains of a slave's lot, 'nights and days' without rest. Both use the merism as 'at any or every time'. The match is real but low in evidential value: day and night are basic inherited words, and a day-night merism is close to universal. Recorded for completeness.

cognate: No cognate is shared between the two anchors. OE weorc = Gk ἔργον (*wérǵom) and OE word = Lat. uerbum (*werdʰom) are cognates, but Plautus uses dictum/factum. The cognate link is only through Greek support (ἔπει ... ἔργῳ; ἔργον τε ἔπος τε).
drift_or_renewal: Latin renews both members (dictum, factum). Greek keeps *werǵom and uses *wekʷos (ἔπος) for 'word'. OE keeps *werǵom and uses *werdʰom.
shared_syntax: Binomial of 'word' and 'deed' joined by a coordinator (OE and, Lat. aut, Gk ἢ ... ἢ / τε ... τε). (In Beo. 289, worda and worca is in the context line after the passage line 288.)
context: Beowulf 287-289: the coast-guard says a sharp warrior must know the difference between words and deeds. Plautus Amph. 169: a slave must be ready whenever a deed or word is needed. Homer: help 'by word or by deed'. All three cover the whole of conduct with this merism. But the merism is universal, and the two anchors share no cognate, so the claim is weak.

support.locus: Buck 1904, Oscan-Umbrian grammar §183 (Umbr. voc. Iupater < *Dieu-pater) and Tab. Iguv. VIa (ueiro pequo castruo fri salua seritu)

cognate: Vocative *ph₂ter in prayer: Gk πάτερ = Lat. pater. The theonym *dyew-: Gk Ζεῦ (vocative) = Lat. Iou- (Iouem, in the same sentence as the Mars invocation, not in apposition; packet lists Iouem as unmapped / no content word). The fused Latin vocative Iupiter (Cato 134) and Umbr. Iupater continue exactly *dyeu ph₂ter, as does Ved. dyaùṣ pítar.
drift_or_renewal: In Cato 141.2 the father-vocative has been moved to another god: Mars pater (also Iane pater in Cato 134). Jupiter is named only in the preliminary wine offering (Ianum Iouemque uino praefamino). Spreading 'pater' to other gods is a known Italic development, and the Latin anchor keeps the formula's shape (god + pater vocative + request) with the theonym renewed. Gk ῥῦσαι 'rescue, guard' may belong with Lat. seruare (*ser-u- 'guard'), which would make the petition verbs cognate too, but that etymology is disputed and not relied on here.
shared_syntax: Vocative theonym + vocative 'father' opening a petitionary prayer, followed by imperative/optative requests to protect: Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ, ἀλλὰ σὺ ῥῦσαι ... ποίησον ... δός; Lat. Mars pater te precor ... uti ... prohibessis defendas auerrunces ... salua seruassis.
context: Both are formal prayers asking the father-god to ward off harm. Ajax asks Zeus to rescue the Achaeans from the mist and give light. Cato's lustration prayer asks Mars to keep off disease, dearth and storms and to keep the herdsmen and the cattle safe (the context sentence has pastores pecuaque salua seruassis, matched exactly by Umbr. ueiro pequo ... salua seritu). The address 'Sky-god father' in a prayer is a well-known inherited formula (recalled). The packet has the Greek form directly, and the Latin passage has its pieces (Iou-, pater) inside a parallel prayer.
phrase: *dyeu ph₂ter (vocative; pie-lex-dyexws + pie-lex-ph2texr) opening a prayer for protection
